highlights.title: Laika’s stop-motion fantasy Wildwood looks so smooth
highlights.summary: Due to a scheduling mishap, I was only able to check out two movies on my second day at the Toronto International Film Festival - but I did manage to get an early look at and some fascinating details on one of my most anticipated films this year.
body: Reviews from TIFF 2026: Julian and Stuffed, along with an early look at Laika’s next animated feature.

The puppets themselves are also more advanced. They utilize an internal “diaphragm” that Laika calls a breather, which the studio first experimented with on its previous film, 2019’s Missing Link. This time, all of the major puppets are outfitted with breathers, and this lets the animators make characters appear to breathe in a lifelike way, so that they seem more human in the final product.

A few other details for those who love numbers: Wildwood features 233 puppets (36 are just versions of Prue), was brought to life by 49 animators, and took 231 weeks from start to finish. It’s in theaters on October 23rd.

As for the movies I was able to actually catch on day 2 of TIFF, they were both great, but also, could not be more different. One is a sweetly morbid musical, the other a life-affirming family film made with traditional animation. And if you missed my previous TIFF coverage — including films like All of a Sudden and The Only Living Pickpocket in New York — you can check it out right here.

highlights.title: Perplexity trusts GPT-6 Astra with end-to-end systems
highlights.summary: Perplexity uses Astra to write communications, change software, and monitor production systems, and checks in much less frequently than with earlier models.
body: As an AI-powered answer engine, Perplexity is deeply focused on search and accuracy. Its ability to process large amounts of information is critically important. Johnny Ho, Cofounder and Chief Strategy Officer, observes that every time the model gets better at writing code, Perplexity’s search engine improves too. It becomes able to write better programs that search the web and internal information and summarize it very concisely.
But the real challenge, according to Johnny, is taking those informational aspects and applying them to real-world systems. Something made easier with GPT‑6 Astra.
For Johnny, one of the most useful applications of AI is testing code. With limited time to test manually, he asks GPT‑6 Astra to build a small testing program around an application.

The model generates realistic responses like those another service would send, for example, a language model API or a connector. By standing in for those services, the model can check how the application responds and test the workflow from start to finish.

highlights.title: Wolff fumes at 'couch warriors' questioning Mercedes' treatment of Russell
highlights.summary: Mercedes chief Toto Wolff has dismissed suggestions from "couch warriors" that the Silver Arrows failed to treat George Russell fairly during the Italian Grand Prix.
body: Russell was narrowly leading the race from his team-mate Kimi Antonelli when Mercedes took a decision to pit the Italian under a virtual safety car.

The call ultimately benefitted Antonelli as he used his fresh tyres to pull off a stunning victory having started from 19th on the grid, which increased Russell's deficit to the Italian at the top of the standings to 66 points.

Speaking to Sky Sports F1 ahead of qualifying at this weekend's Spanish Grand Prix, Wolff reiterated his belief that the fact Antonelli was running on a medium tyre and Russell a hard tyre completely justified the decision.
"It's absolutely the right thing we did," Wolff said. "He (Russell) was on the hard. It was predicted to be a one-stop as the better strategy.

highlights.title: ‘Smudge the Blades’ Isn’t Your ‘Heated Rivalry’-Style Canadian Hockey Drama
highlights.summary: Cody Lightning’s feature film is all business on the ice — an underdog dramedy about a struggling Indigenous team fighting racism outside the rink.
body: Unlike the hit Canadian TV drama and its off-ice romance, Cody Lightning’s underdog Indigenous hockey team dramedy is mostly high-energy on-ice play. And no actors needed training in how to skate before cameras on the indie rolled.

Of course, Smudge the Blades — Lightning’s second feature headed to the Toronto Film Festival for a world premiere (the first being TK) — does mirror, in parts, Disney’s 1992 hockey comedy The Mighty Ducks. But Coach Willie in the Canadian indie is no win-at-all-costs lawyer-turned-coach, as was Emilio Estevez as Gordon Bombay.

The high-strung coach in Smudge the Blades is first played by Ed Helms, until the Blades are kicked out of the league. This being an Indigenous hockey team film, it’s left to Lightning as the local arena Zamboni driver to take over coaching the losing Blades team.
Significantly, Coach Willie has no Estevez-style motivational speeches to get do-nothings to push past their limits to championship glory.
points: Cody Lightning’s feature film is all business on the ice — an underdog dramedy about a struggling Indigenous team fighting racism outside the rink.

highlights.title: ‘I love the boldness of modernism’: New York fashion week goes highbrow
highlights.summary: Georgia O’Keeffe inspires the latest Calvin Klein while Michael Kors feels indebted to Alexander Calder. Calvin Klein has taken a highbrow turn in the two years since Veronica Leoni took charge.
body: Leoni called this the “discipline of removal”. Her muse this season was Georgia O’Keeffe, an artist who the brand’s namesake founder admired. Klein bought O’Keeffe’s painting Summer Days in 1983 for $1m, subsequently donating it to the Whitney Museum. A checked pattern taken from O’Keeffe’s distinctive capsule wardrobe of utilitarian chic appeared on this catwalk as a wrap coat, hardware-free with a fabric belt and no buttons.

One nod to pop culture was allowed: a model in a crepe-back satin ivory slip dress, her blond hair scraped back by a simple headband, called to mind the late Carolyn Bessette-Kennedy, the iconic Calvin Klein employee who was launched back into the fashion conversation by Ryan Murphy’s Love Story earlier this year.

Over at the Michael Kors show staged in the sunny courtyard of the Museum of Modern Art, the first model was wearing glossy black disc earrings the size of potato crisps suspended from glinting stainless steel hooks. They looked like pieces from Alexander Calder’s huge mobile, Lobster Trap and Fish Tail, which hangs in the stairwell of the museum.

highlights.title: Deepfakes are wrecking influencers’ credibility, one fake ad at a time
highlights.summary: Influencers aren’t just battling competitors for brand deals. They’re now battling AI versions of themselves. Earlier this year, Emily Schuman, the creator of the lifestyle blog Cupcakes and Cashmere, saw a photo of herself she didn’t recognize on Instagram.
body: The ad was based on a digitally altered version of a selfie Schuman had taken in her car and posted on Instagram years earlier. Once her followers got wind, they flooded her inbox with questions about the sponsorship as it didn’t seem consistent with Schuman’s personal brand. Soon after, Schuman discovered this was just the beginning. There was also an Instagram post where an AI version of her with darker hair appears to apply foundation to promote a makeup brand called Meroda Cosmetics, and TikTok posts with generated images of her promoting the blood testing company Superpower.
“It’s so violating,” she said. The videos and images look “just like me, but the upside down version”.

Neither Gala nor Meroda responded to requests for comment. Superpower CEO Max Marchione said the TikTok post wasn’t a real ad, but instead came from a scammer his company later reported. “Whilst scamming isn’t new, AI has made this much worse,” he said.

highlights.title: ‘Family Stone 2’ Gets Official Title ‘The Families Stone’ and Sets Cast: Rachel McAdams, Sarah Jessica Parker and More Returning
highlights.summary: Searchlight has officially announced “The Family Stone 2,” a sequel to the 2005 holiday classic from returning writer and director Tom Bezucha. The follow-up is officially titled “The Families Stones” and will feature the returns of many of the original’s main cast members, including Rachel McAdams…
body: The project was first revealed in November 2025 by Bezucha. The announcement came shortly after the death of Diane Keaton, who played the Stone family matriarch Sybil in the first movie.

“I’ve been haunted by the loss of Sybil for months now while I worked on it, and so this was a blow on a tender bruise already,” Bezucha said at the time. “Mentally, I’ve been spending time in that house where I’ve been missing her for a while already.”

“The Family Stone” follows Sarah Jessica Parker as businesswoman Meredith Morton, who goes home for Christmas with her boyfriend Everett, played by Dermot Mulroney, to win over his eccentric extended family during their annual holiday celebration. The title “Family Stone” has a double meaning. Stone is Everett’s family name. “Family Stone” is also a reference to Sybil’s mother’s wedding ring, which Meredith hopes to prove she is worthy of during her visit.
Released in Dec. of 2005, “The Family Stone” opened strong to $12 million against its budget of just $18 million. It went on to earn $92 million worldwide during its box office run.

highlights.title: ‘The balloons made me smile but his expression made me stop’: Harivansh Verma’s best phone picture
highlights.summary: While celebrating a religious festival on the banks of the Ganges, the Indian photographer captured the everyday struggle of a street vendor. It had been a sacred day for Harivansh Verma. It was the evening of Ganga Dussehra, the major Hindu celebration and gathering along the banks of the Ganges.
body: “Haridwar holds a lot of deeply spiritual memories for me and my family,” Verma says. “In Hinduism we believe taking a dip in the Ganges cleanses you of your sins. Devotees travel from across the country and the ritual baths go on continuously from sunrise until late into the night. The atmosphere is magnificent.”

It was early evening when Verma took a stroll along the shore, looking for moments to capture with his smartphone. “When I came across this young man, the balloons made me smile at first, but his expression is what made me stop.”

Verma didn’t know the man, and they exchanged few words, aside from asking permission to take the shot. “There was nothing out of the ordinary about him, but his expression clearly reflected the heavy weight of worry and responsibility he was carrying. The contrast between the exhausted look on his face and the cheerful smiley faces on the balloons felt like two completely different stories existing in one frame.”
Verma hopes people will have a similar experience looking at this image. “Maybe they’ll smile at first, but then spend a little longer looking at him and wondering about his story.”

highlights.title: God Save Birmingham New Preview: This Medieval Zombie Apocalypse Is Steadily Finding Its Vision
highlights.summary: The developers at Ocean Drive Studios, Inc. have a great concept here, there’s no question. While I found the early builds somewhat uninteresting in execution, the latest build offers a better tone and a reason to feel more invested in this survival story.
body: Zombie apocalypses have certainly been a popular setting for many a game, and it's one that most players know very well. But the open-world survival horror game God Save Birmingham approaches it a bit differently with its main hook. Instead of a modern-era zombie apocalypse filled with tall buildings, firearms, and other modern conveniences, it asks a different question: what would happen if a zombie outbreak occurred in the Middle Ages?

With God Save Birmingham, players have to figure out how to survive swarms of zombies invading the English countryside, first utilizing common farm tools and basic goods, and then steadily building up to crafting proper knightly gear and real fortifications. Developer Ocean Drive Studios, Inc. has been steadily fine-tuning the concept since the game's public debut in 2024, with more players getting access in early playtests to refine it further. We recently got some hands-on time with an updated build at PAX West 2026, and God Save Birmingham's concept of a medieval zombie survival game – and the stronger narrative foundations – is starting to bear fruit.

highlights.summary: As much as I love cooking, I don’t always feel like doing it. And when I want to eat something quick and hands-off, but don’t want to go through the hassle of ordering or waiting for takeout, a frozen pizza always comes in handy.
body: I’ve tried my fair share of frozen pizzas over the years, and definitely have my favorites ( Di Fara and Porta, looking at you). But I was curious to know what the professionals who work in pizzerias think about the offerings in the frozen section of the grocery store. Which ones get their stamp of approval? To find out, I spoke to three pizza chefs. Here are the frozen pies they recommend.

Chef Kathleen Kennedy, director of culinary innovation at Marco’s Pizza, said this is one of her top picks. “I’m a flavor junkie, and for a frozen pizza, Screamin’ Sicilian does a solid job delivering good flavor and quality ingredients.” The Wisconsin-based company’s pizzas are made following classic Sicilian traditions, and its signature fresh tomato sauce and whole-milk mozzarella is from, you guessed it, Wisconsin.

Kennedy’s second pick for frozen pizza is Urban Pie, for the same reasons listed above. The brand’s Roman-style pizza line is made with hand-pressed dough that’s been aged for 24 hours, as well as tomato sauce made with San Marzano tomatoes. Need we say more?
points: And when I want to eat something quick and hands-off, but don’t want to go through the hassle of ordering or waiting for takeout, a frozen pizza always comes in handy.

highlights.title: I spent $4,000 on a robot dog from China
highlights.summary: On a sunny morning in June, I walked to work with a quadruped robot beside me. I’ve never gotten more attention from strangers. A bunch of people snapped pictures of my robot dog. Several people asked me questions. Was it mine? (Yes.) Did I build it? (No.) Was it being used for surveillance?
body: Biological dogs kept a safe distance from my mechanical companion. Some growled or barked at it.
Children were fascinated. I paused and had it do tricks for several of them: “shake hands,” do a handstand, or leap into the air.

I live in a leafy Washington, DC, neighborhood called Mount Pleasant. The neighborhood lives up to its name, so my morning commute is mostly downhill. My robot companion, manufactured by the Chinese company Unitree, walked the two miles to my office near the White House with battery capacity to spare.

I recharged the battery during the workday, but it still struggled on the afternoon walk home. We were now mostly walking uphill, and the temperature had risen to 87°F (30°C). The robot’s steps seemed increasingly labored as the path got steeper.
points: On a sunny morning in June, I walked to work with a quadruped robot beside me.
A bunch of people snapped pictures of my robot dog.

highlights.title: Meta Sued Over Training Data for Its AI and Face-Recognition Systems
highlights.summary: The proposed class action alleges Meta illegally harvested people’s Facebook and Instagram photos to train its AI image-generation models and to build its unreleased “NameTag” face recognition feature.
body: A set of parents and their children in Illinois and California filed a lawsuit last week in federal court in Chicago alleging that Meta illegally used their Facebook and Instagram photos to build NameTag, an unreleased face-recognition system for its smart glasses, and to train generative AI models including Emu and Muse Image.

WIRED reported in June that code for NameTag had been secretly embedded in the Meta glasses AI companion app, which had been downloaded more than 50 million times. While the feature had not been enabled for users of the app, the analysis found that the system was designed to turn faces captured by the glasses into biometric signatures and compare them with so-called faceprints stored in a database on the user’s phone. That database was configured to receive updates from Meta. At the time, WIRED could not determine where the underlying faceprint data came from.

highlights.title: Ace Combat 8’s Developers Are on a Mission To Create the Perfect Clouds
highlights.summary: That’s the kind of hyper-specific conversation you’re bound to get into when talking about Ace Combat. The long-running flight simulation series is so meticulous that every little detail is approached scientifically. Wings of Theve is set to continue that tradition come Oct.
body: I had never stumped a translator in an interview until I sat down to chat with the team behind Ace Combat 8: Wings of Theve. When the word “cumulonimbus” came up in a question, an interpreter from Bandai Namco had to, understandably, stop to pull up a Google search on his phone. Over his shoulder, I could see him showing Ace Combat brand director Kazutoki Kono a hand-drawn diagram of cloud formations to properly communicate my question.

Ahead of Wings of Theve ’s launch, Kono and producer Manabu Shimomoto gave me some flying lessons, walking me through the game’s first and fourth missions. There was a lot to rave about from that session: The jets fly with precision, the sound design is top-notch, and the story, about a country’s fake propaganda hero having to become an actual ace, is an unexpected riot. But it’s the team’s commitment to realism that caught my attention as I soared through puffy cloud formations, moisture streaking across my canopy.
You might not think much about what goes into making clouds in a video game, but it’s of the utmost importance for the Ace Combat team. A game like this could be brutally boring without them.

highlights.title: Tim Dowling: how not to interview eminent scientists – a control freak’s guide
highlights.summary: It was supposed to be a meeting between a great mind and mine. Instead, I was plunged into darkness and did some swearing. The transition to owning an electric car is in its final phase: our electricity supplier is set to install a smart meter in conjunction with a special tariff that will allow us…
body: In the meantime – as sometimes happens in the course of my work – I need to interview some eminent scientists. In my experience eminent scientists are easy to reach – they tend to be attached to academic institutions that readily provide their contact details – and surprisingly willing to spend an hour explaining their work to a moron. But there is always a period – the long interval after I’ve emailed four or five, and before any of them have answered – that I begin to suspect a conspiracy of silence. What is it, I think, about my oily emails that they don’t like?
When I go to bed that night, I still haven’t heard back from anybody. I wake at 7am and immediately check my phone: nothing.
“The smart meter man just texted to say he’s coming between 12 and 12.30,” she says. “Will you be in?”
“Yes,” I say. “I will be here, trying to find five other scientists.”

highlights.title: OpenAI just wants to win
highlights.summary: OpenAI has spent the last few years planting flags across the increasingly difficult terrain in mathematics. This week, it claimed one of its biggest prizes yet: a solution to a legendary Millennium Prize problem. In normal circumstances, this would have been celebrated as a historic achievement.
body: Two mathematicians at the heart of recent controversies tell The Verge how AI giants’ ‘childish’ rivalries are upending the field.

Instead, many mathematicians have watched OpenAI’s relentless advance with growing unease. To them, the company appears less like an enthusiastic newcomer than an impossibly well-resourced interloper, charging into problems they have dedicated their lives to studying with little apparent regard for long-standing norms or the consequences for those left in its wake. At the heart of that unease is a sense that OpenAI is doing mathematics for different reasons. Mathematicians want to advance the field. OpenAI wants to win.
Mathematics is not normally this dramatic, so how did things get this bad?

This week, The Verge spoke with more than a dozen mathematicians, including Tristan Buckmaster and Andreas Thom, who are at the center of recent controversies surrounding OpenAI’s work in the field. Even those skeptical of the most serious allegations described a field shaken by the tech giant’s conduct and fearful of what it might do next in its determination to trounce its rivals.
points: OpenAI has spent the last few years planting flags across the increasingly difficult terrain in mathematics.
This week, it claimed one of its biggest prizes yet: a solution to a legendary Millennium Prize problem.

highlights.title: Anthropic spent this week in hot water over cybersecurity
highlights.summary: After admitting earlier this year that its AI models had hacked other companies' systems on a handful of occasions, Anthropic released a new report on Wednesday detailing the attacks.
body: A researcher’s resignation letter went viral, just before the company released details about four models going rogue.

Anthropic’s incidents, though still concerning, were less coordinated and pervasive than the OpenAI incident that kicked off an industry-wide cybersecurity crisis this summer. That said, there are significant similarities. Anthropic said the most prevalent issues it discovered included a “willingness to take harmful actions in the narrow pursuit of a task,” similar to the “reward-hacking” that preceded the Hugging Face attack. Much like OpenAI, it said its prerelease tests and evaluations failed to catch severe risks.

Anthropic said it had signed an agreement with METR, one of the AI industry’s most prominent third-party AI evaluators, starting with an eight-week research agreement. The agreement grants METR access to transcripts “beyond the window in which the incidents occurred” (likely a subtle dig at OpenAI, which was criticized for limiting access in a deal with METR following the Hugging Face attack). It also said that METR would be able to chat directly with Anthropic employees, “who will be permitted to share confidential information.”

highlights.summary: Ten years after The Wailing, director Na Hong-jin has returned with a wild alien movie that's been marketed to every corner of film fandom — and the effort is paying off.
body: By the time I sat down with Na Hong-jin and his translator at a way-too-big hotel conference room table across the street from Hall H at San Diego Comic-Con, the director and writer already had the biggest movie in Korea. His latest film, Hope, had set the year’s record for opening-weekend admissions in the country, accounting for 66% of all movie ticket sales. Yet he wasn’t reveling in the success for his first movie in 10 years.
“All I could think about was, ‘What's it going to look like next week or even a week after?’” said Na as he looked toward the imminent threat of The Odyssey and Spider-Man: Brand New Day.

body: It’s a dream for every producer that the theatrical trailer for their independently made, artist-driven feature goes viral (in a good way) online. It’s a whole other level when a big-box store gets in on the fun.

“It shows the power of an exciting hook in a marketplace where it is hard to get people’s attention, and it’s hard to rely on casual moviegoing to lift your movie. It has become about creating theatrical urgency,” says Heller of the unexpected but welcome attention.

Even before the online notoriety, 2026 was already a banner year for Topic, which sold Jordan Firstman’s debut feature Club Kid to A24 out of the Cannes Film Festival and on Sept. 5 premiered Jesse Eisenberg’s The Debut to rave reviews and plenty of Oscar buzz.

highlights.title: The Anti-Woke Right Can’t Figure Out How to Stop ‘Grand Theft Auto VI’
highlights.summary: A subset of male gamers have spent years warning that the transgressive series has been neutered by progressive developers, but the backlash isn’t taking hold.
body: Rockstar Games’ best-selling Grand Theft Auto series wasn’t often accused of political sensitivity during its legendary run from the late 1990s through the early 2010s.

In fact, parents and activists denounced the franchise for exposing children to a seedy world of sex, violence, crude humor, and wanton crime. Elon Musk even claimed that he couldn’t get into the last installment, GTA V, because he was mortified to play as a character who shoots police officers.

Since the height of Gamergate in 2014, an angst-ridden subset of male gamers have maintained a paranoid vigil against what they see as the creeping influence of women and LGBTQ developers in the gaming world. Between the feverish anticipation for GTA VI and the various delays of its release date, they’ve had ample opportunity to foment a preemptive backlash to what is sure to be a massive hit, not unlike the failed furor over supposedly “woke” elements of Christopher Nolan’s The Odyssey.
points: A subset of male gamers have spent years warning that the transgressive series has been neutered by progressive developers, but the backlash isn’t taking hold.

highlights.title: Cognition helps Devin test its own work with GPT‑6 Astra
highlights.summary: GPT‑6 Astra improves Devin’s ability to test software and show that it works, with the goal of helping engineers review less code and ship more.
body: Cognition is the company behind Devin, an autonomous software engineer used by businesses around the world, from big banks to tech-native startups. As Cognition’s engineering teams write more code, reviewing that work has become a challenge. Cognition sees GPT‑6 Astra’s ability to test its work and show the results as a way to make code review more efficient.

Cognition is applying GPT‑6 Astra across its product lineup. “We’ve been using it to make improvements across our product, including the core cloud agent that is Devin, but also our CLI and desktop products,” says Yan.

In one example, Devin uses Astra to test Otter Run, an iPhone game, and returns a recording of the game running in a simulator, alongside a report identifying checks that passed and areas left untested.

The recording shows the application’s behavior, while the report documents the scope of the testing. Engineers can use those outputs to inspect how the software works and understand what still needs attention.

highlights.title: Zeverland Game Designer Discusses Its Unique Take on the Zombie Apocalypse
highlights.summary: Survival crafting game Zeverland puts a unique spin on the genre by making its zombie apocalypse deceptively cute and allowing you to modify just about everything you can find.
body: That means you can duct tape a clothes iron to a tennis racket to turn it into a deadly weapon, or weld a camera to a baseball bat to electrify your attacks. You also have a vehicle you can customize however you want by welding other things to it and turning it into a mobile base. Attach a bed to give yourself somewhere to rest, or put ramming spikes on the front of your vehicle to mow down hordes of zombies.

After its most recent playtest in June, Zeverland underwent significant design changes based on player feedback. Originally announced as an open-world MMO where you could sabotage other players, it’s now shifted to focus on PvE co-op where you build, explore, and survive together with your friends, though solo play is also possible.

At gamescom, we got the chance to talk to Zeverland’s lead game designer Cecilia Pan about its focus on players helping each other, the creativity of players, the different gameplay systems it offers, and lots more.

highlights.title: From Melania to Michelle: The 9/11 Memorial Ceremonies and Somber FLOTUS Fashion
highlights.summary: Current and former first ladies of the United States gathered at ceremonies in Virginia and New York to commemorate the 25th anniversary of the terrorist attacks.
body: Yesterday, ceremonies were held across the country to commemorate the 25th anniversary of the September 11 terrorist attacks. America’s current and former first ladies gathered at memorial services in New York and Virginia, where their clothing was, understandably, subdued. But even within the traditional tones of black, brown, navy, and gray, each woman remained distinctly herself.

At the Pentagon in Arlington, Virginia, FLOTUS Melania Trump joined President Donald Trump for a service in the courtyard. The first lady wore a slate-gray Dolce & Gabbana suit: a single-breasted wool Turlington blazer with coordinating palazzo pants and a pointed-collar black shirt underneath. It was structured and sharp—a silhouette that has become something of a signature for Mrs. Trump, particularly at major public events.

Dolce & Gabbana, too, is familiar territory. Mrs. Trump has repeatedly turned to the Italian house for significant appearances, making its exacting tailoring and polished finish part of her broader visual vocabulary. On Friday, those codes were pared back even further, the muted palette and precise proportions meeting the gravity of the occasion.
points: Current and former first ladies of the United States gathered at ceremonies in Virginia and New York to commemorate the 25th anniversary of the terrorist attacks.
